title: Review 85: Maintaining Systems or Redesigning Them? 2026
author: Chris Jones
summary: Jones argues that many pressures school leaders experience are design problems rather than performance problems, and that sustainable improvement comes from coherence among curriculum, staffing, timetabling, assessment and capacity, not from adding initiatives and monitoring. He notes that improvement strategies tend to be additive, so complexity grows faster than coherence and staff spend their energy holding fragmented systems together. The strongest schools, he says, are not the busiest but the clearest, with lower cognitive load for staff and fairer, more predictable experiences for pupils. He treats curriculum as organisational architecture and the timetable as an honest expression of school values. His EPR process asks leaders to evaluate honestly, plan, then evaluate risk by asking what happens if they act and what happens if they do not. He closes by naming permanent reactivity as a major risk and strategic courage as the leadership demand.
points: Many school pressures are design problems, so asking staff to work harder cannot solve structural overload.
Additive improvement (more interventions, monitoring and procedures) produces fragmentation, which shows up as absence, weak retention and harder behaviour.
Curriculum decisions shape staffing, timetabling and workload, so redesign has to be done across these together.
The EPR process asks Evaluate, Plan, then Evaluate Risk, including the risk of not changing a structurally unsustainable system.
Coherence is a leadership priority because it reduces friction and creates human capacity.
quotes: The challenge is often structural. The system itself has become increasingly difficult to sustain.
Each individual response may be understandable. But collectively, schools can gradually create environments where complexity expands faster than coherence.
Schools cannot continually solve systemic pressure by asking increasingly stretched professionals simply to work harder. There comes a point where the deeper issue is no longer effort. It is design.

We see curriculum as organisational architecture. The moment a school decides what matters educationally, it also begins shaping how time, staffing, resources and relationships will operate across the whole organisation.
The timetable is not simply a grid. It is a reflection of organisational design.

The second question is often neglected in education. Schools become understandably cautious about change because of perceived risk. Yet maintaining structurally unsustainable systems also carries risk, sometimes far greater risk over time.
The schools that thrive long term are rarely those doing the most. They are usually the ones that have designed most thoughtfully.
Ultimately, great school design is not about efficiency for its own sake. It is about creating human capacity.
